title: Novena for When God Seems Silent
kicker: 9 days of prayer in spiritual dryness
card: For anyone whose prayer feels empty, whose Mass feels like nothing, or who feels God has gone quiet: 9 days of staying with Him.
ogDescription: 9 days of prayer in spiritual dryness, through Our Lady, St. Jane de Chantal, St. Francis de Sales and St. Thérèse.
description: A 9-day Catholic novena for spiritual dryness, when prayer feels empty and God seems silent, through St. Jane de Chantal, St. Francis de Sales and St. Thérèse.

epigraph.text: My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and behold the face of God?

closingVerse.text: Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; yea, wait for the LORD!

printClosing: Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage;

saints.name: St. Jane Frances de Chantal
saints.bio: Widowed at 28 with 4 young children, she founded the Visitation nuns with St. Francis de Sales. For 41 years she suffered temptations against faith, yet kept praying and hoping in God.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Jane Frances de Chantal in a black veil and white wimple, with a silver cross
saints.openingRole: who hoped in You through long years of darkness

saints.name: St. Francis de Sales
saints.bio: Bishop of Geneva and gentle guide of souls. As a student in Paris he was sure God had rejected him, until he prayed the Memorare before a statue of Our Lady and the fear lifted.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Francis de Sales, bearded, in a dark cape with a pectoral cross
saints.openingRole: who chose to love You when he felt only fear

saints.name: St. Thérèse of Lisieux
saints.bio: A French Carmelite who died at 24. In her last 18 months, heaven seemed walled off and brought her no comfort, yet she kept choosing to believe and to love.
saints.openingRole: who believed when heaven seemed closed to her

openingPrayer: Heavenly Father, You are near even when we cannot feel You. Prayer has gone dry, Mass seems empty, and You seem silent. We come anyway, wanting to stay with You. Teach us to love You for Yourself and not for what we feel. Today we ask Our Lady of Solitude, who kept faith on Holy Saturday; St. Jane Frances de Chantal, who hoped in You through long years of darkness; St. Francis de Sales, who chose to love You when he felt only fear; and St. Thérèse of Lisieux, who believed when heaven seemed closed to her, to join their prayers with ours, through Christ our Lord.
closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, You knew the darkness of Gethsemane and of the cross. Stay with us when God seems silent, keep us faithful when we feel nothing, and bring us at last to see You face to face.

tips.p: One person leads each part; all respond pray for us and Amen, and say the closing prayers together. The prayers say “we”; if you pray alone, say “I”.

Keep going to Mass during these 9 days, and to Confession if you can, even when you feel nothing: grace does not depend on feelings. Keep a prayer time you can manage, and keep it faithfully even when it feels empty. If you can, talk it over with a priest or spiritual director. Sometimes dryness invites a change, such as a sin we hold on to or a life with no room for God; often it is simply a season God allows. Either way, it is not a sign that God has left you, and He can use it to draw you closer.

tips.h: When it may be more than dryness
tips.p: Dryness touches prayer; sometimes the heaviness reaches everything. If, for 2 weeks or more, you have also lost interest in things you used to enjoy, sleep or eat very differently, or feel hopeless or worthless, please talk to a doctor as well as a priest. Both can be true at once, and getting help is never a lack of faith. If you ever think of harming yourself, reach out right away to someone you trust or a crisis helpline.

intentionPlaceholder: Write what feels dry or silent, or the person you are praying for.

days.title: When God Seems Far
days.verse: Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him; on the left hand I seek him, but I cannot behold him; I turn to the right hand, but I cannot see him. But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
days.refl: Job looks everywhere for God, forward and backward, left and right, and finds nothing. Many of us know that search. Prayer that once felt warm now feels like talking to the ceiling, and words we used to love sound empty. Job does not pretend otherwise, and neither do we have to. Yet in the same breath he says, “He knows the way that I take.” We may not see God, but He sees us. So we begin these nine days honestly, bringing Him the silence itself.
days.more: The Church has a name for this: dryness. The Catechism describes it as a time when the heart finds no taste in thoughts, memories or feelings, even spiritual ones, and calls it “the moment of sheer faith clinging faithfully to Jesus in his agony and in his tomb” (CCC 2731). It is not a strange or rare trial. Countless saints have walked this road, and Jesus Himself knew the anguish of Gethsemane and the cross.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, we have looked for You and cannot feel You near. Our prayers seem to go nowhere, and the silence is heavy. We will not pretend with You. We bring You this dryness just as it is, and we trust that You know the way we take, even when we cannot see You. Stay with us through these nine days. Our Lady of Solitude, who waited in faith when all seemed silent, pray for us.
days.step: Choose a time and place to pray each day of this novena, short enough to keep, and keep it even when nothing seems to happen.

days.title: Led Into the Desert
days.verse: Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.
days.refl: Through the prophet Hosea, God speaks of His people as a bride He longs to win back. And where does He take her? Into the wilderness, to “speak tenderly to her.” In Scripture the desert is where God led Israel for forty years, fed them with manna and taught them to trust Him. A dry season can feel like punishment, or like proof that we have failed. Hosea shows another meaning: the desert can be where God draws us close, away from everything that used to fill us.
days.more: St. Jane Frances de Chantal knew this desert. A widow who founded the Visitation nuns with St. Francis de Sales, she was troubled by temptations against faith for most of her life, forty-one years by her own count. St. Vincent de Paul, who knew her well, said she was full of faith even while thoughts against it tormented her. The darkness did not make her less holy. She became a saint in it.
days.prayer: Lord, when this dryness feels like punishment, remind us that You lead Your people into the desert to speak to their hearts. If something in us needs to change, show us gently. If this is simply a season You allow, help us not to run from it. Speak tenderly to us here, even if we cannot yet hear You. St. Jane Frances de Chantal, who stayed faithful in the dark, pray for us.
days.step: Ask yourself honestly whether anything is crowding God out of your life. If so, name one thing to change; if not, thank Him for leading you here.

days.title: When We Cannot Pray
days.verse: “Be still, and know that I am God. I am exalted among the nations, I am exalted in the earth!”
days.refl: In the middle of a psalm about earthquakes, roaring seas and nations in uproar, God speaks: “Be still, and know that I am God.” He does not ask for many words or strong feelings. He asks us to stop and let Him be God. When prayer has gone dry, we often try harder, or we give up. There is a third way: simply to stay. Sitting quietly before Him, even distracted, even feeling nothing, is real prayer.
days.more: St. Francis de Sales gave this counsel for dry prayer: do not be disturbed by the dryness, however great it is, and stay calmly before God anyway. He pointed to courtiers who went to court a hundred times with no hope of a word from their king, only to pay their respects and be seen by him. Our faithfulness in staying is itself an act of love, and God sees us there.
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, when we do not know how to pray, pray in us. When words dry up and feelings are gone, teach us simply to stay with You, still and attentive, letting You be God. Take our distracted, empty minutes and make them a gift of love. We would rather sit before You with nothing than go anywhere else. St. Francis de Sales, gentle teacher of prayer, pray for us.
days.step: Spend five quiet minutes before God today, in a church if you can. When your mind wanders, gently come back. Nothing needs to happen.

days.title: When Mass Feels Like Nothing
days.verse: Jesus said to the twelve, “Will you also go away?” Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life; and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”
days.refl: Jesus had just told the crowds that He would give His flesh to eat, and many walked away. Turning to the twelve, He asked, “Will you also go away?” Peter did not say that everything made sense or felt wonderful. He said, “Lord, to whom shall we go?” Some Sundays, Mass can feel like going through the motions: we stand, sit and kneel and feel nothing at all. Peter’s answer can be ours. We stay, because no one else has the words of eternal life.
days.more: Our feelings do not make Jesus present at Mass, and they cannot make Him absent. The Church teaches that the whole Christ is truly, really and substantially present in the Eucharist (CCC 1374), and that the sacraments act by Christ’s own saving work, not by the holiness or feelings of those who receive them (CCC 1128). On a dry Sunday, the same Lord is on the altar, and our coming is a gift to Him.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are truly present in the Eucharist, whether we feel You or not. Forgive us when we come to Mass distracted or cold, and thank You for drawing us back anyway. When it all feels like routine, give us Peter’s simple faith: to whom else would we go? Let every Mass we attend, even the driest, become an act of love, of trust and of thanks to You.
days.step: Go to Mass this week, or visit the Blessed Sacrament. When the Host is raised, quietly pray Peter’s words: “Lord, to whom shall we go?”

days.title: When Fear Says God Has Left
days.verse: For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
days.refl: Dryness can slide into fear: maybe God has given up on us; maybe we were never really His. St. Paul answers with one of the strongest promises in Scripture. Nothing, not death, not powers, not anything else in all creation, can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. Our feelings are part of creation too. A heart that feels nothing cannot cut us off from Him. His love does not rise and fall with our moods. It holds us even when we cannot feel held.
days.more: As a student in Paris, the young Francis de Sales became convinced that God had destined him to be lost forever. For weeks it tormented him. Even then he prayed that, whatever happened, he might at least love God in this life. At last, in the church of Saint-Étienne-des-Grès he knelt before a statue of Our Lady and prayed the Memorare, and the fear lifted. We pray that same prayer every day of this novena.
days.prayer: Father, when fear whispers that You have turned away from us, let us hear St. Paul instead: nothing can separate us from Your love in Christ Jesus. Quiet our anxious hearts. If we cannot feel Your love today, let us at least choose to love You. Mary, our Mother, we come to you as St. Francis de Sales did, trusting that no one who asks your help is left unaided. Pray for us.
days.step: When fear comes today, pray the Memorare slowly, as St. Francis de Sales did, and then leave the fear with Mary.

days.title: Believing Without Seeing
days.verse: Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe.”
days.refl: Thomas would not believe until he could see and touch. When Jesus came, He did not send him away; He let Thomas see. Then He spoke of us: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe.” We live inside that blessing. Faith is not a feeling of warmth or certainty; it is trusting God’s word when we see nothing. In dryness, an act of faith made without any feeling is no less real. It may even be a purer gift.
days.more: St. Thérèse of Lisieux lived this beatitude. From Easter 1896 until her death, the thought of heaven, once her joy, brought her no comfort; she wrote that it was like a wall rising to the heavens. When she sang of heaven, she said, she sang only of what she wished to believe. Yet she wrote that she had made more acts of faith in that year than in all the rest of her life.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You call blessed those who have not seen and yet believe. We cannot see You, and often we cannot feel You, but we choose to believe. Take each small act of faith we make in the dark and let it be a gift of love. When doubts press in, help our unbelief and hold us close. St. Thérèse, who believed when heaven seemed closed to you, pray for us.
days.step: Pray the Creed slowly today, or say “Jesus, I believe in You” several times, without waiting to feel it.

days.title: Walking in the Dark
days.verse: Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant, who walks in darkness and has no light, yet trusts in the name of the LORD and relies upon his God?
days.refl: Isaiah describes a faithful person who still “walks in darkness and has no light.” This is not someone who has lost God or done something wrong. It is someone who fears the LORD and obeys Him. The prophet’s counsel is simple: trust in the name of the LORD and lean on your God. In the dark, we do not need to see the whole road. We need the next step, taken with our hand in His, and faithfulness in small daily things.
days.more: St. Jane Frances de Chantal walked this way for years. In one letter she wrote, “Notwithstanding my absolute misery I hope in Him.” St. Francis de Sales, her spiritual director, assured her that bare, dry acts of the will, made without any feeling, are among the highest worship we can give. So she kept going, leading her sisters and founding new convents, trusting God in the dark.
days.prayer: Lord, when we walk in darkness and have no light, teach us to trust in Your name and lean on You. We do not ask to see the whole road, only to take the next step with You. Keep us faithful in our daily prayer and our ordinary duties, even when they feel empty. St. Jane Frances de Chantal, who hoped in God through long years of darkness, pray for us.
days.step: Choose one small prayer or duty you have been neglecting because it feels pointless, and do it today as an act of trust.

days.title: The Seed in the Dark
days.verse: Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
days.refl: A seed does its most important work buried in dark soil, where no one sees it. Jesus says it must fall into the earth and die to bear fruit. He spoke first of His own death, but His words also describe what God often does in us. Dryness can feel like something dying: old consolations, old ways of praying, our sense of being good at faith. Yet below the surface, God may be making room for a deeper, quieter love that bears much fruit.
days.more: St. John of the Cross, the great teacher of the “dark night,” explained that God sometimes takes away the sweetness we once found in prayer so that we learn to love Him for Himself and not for His gifts. What feels like loss can be God’s own work. Not every dry season is that night, and a priest can help us tell. But no time given to God is ever wasted.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You fell into the earth like a grain of wheat and rose to give new life. When our prayer feels as if it is dying, help us trust that You are at work where we cannot see. Strip away whatever we love more than You, even our good feelings, and grow in us a quieter, deeper love. Let this dry season bear fruit in Your time and in Your way.
days.step: Remember one way you grew during a past hard season. Thank God for it, and ask Him to do that same hidden work in you now.

days.title: Hope and Thanks
days.verse: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my help and my God.
days.refl: The psalmist speaks to his own soul: “Why are you cast down?” He does not deny how low he feels. But he tells himself what to do next: “Hope in God; for I shall again praise him.” The psalm that began with a soul thirsting for God ends in hope. We may finish this novena still feeling dry; God has not promised us a timeline. But we can thank Him for staying with us, notice the graces He gave, and place this season in His hands.
days.more: The saints of this novena did not wait for feelings to return before they praised God. St. Jane Frances de Chantal hoped in Him through years of darkness. St. Francis de Sales chose to love Him when he felt only fear. St. Thérèse kept believing when heaven seemed closed. Our Lady stood by the cross and kept faith through the silence of Holy Saturday. Their hope rested on God’s faithfulness, and so can ours.
days.prayer: Lord, on this ninth day we thank You for staying with us through every dry and silent hour of this novena, and for every grace, seen and unseen. Thank you, Our Lady of Solitude, St. Jane Frances de Chantal, St. Francis de Sales and St. Thérèse, for carrying our prayers to Jesus. Father, we place this season in Your hands. Whether consolation comes soon, or late, or only when we see You face to face, let us hope in You and praise You again. Your will be done.
days.step: Write down three graces you noticed during these nine days, and thank God for them together.
